title: Safety in the Classroom
summary: Staying healthy and safe when using computers: posture, eye strain and repetitive strain, hazards in the computer room, and what employers must do to protect their staff.
learn: Back problems, eye strain and RSI, and how to avoid them
intro: How to keep the equipment, your data and yourself safe when using computers: backache, eye strain and RSI, ergonomics, threats to data and the laws employers must follow.

pages.spec: Know the three things we keep safe when using computers and what a hazard is
pages.summary: When using ICT we must keep the equipment, our data and ourselves safe. A hazard is anything that could cause damage, harm or ill health. Most safety rules are common sense, and anything dangerous should be reported.

blocks.text: When you use computers, there are **three** things you need to keep safe:

items: **The equipment**: the computers, screens, keyboards and cables.
**Our data**: our files, work and personal information.
**Ourselves**: our bodies and our health.

blocks.text: We follow **[[health and safety]]** rules to keep ourselves from harm. Most of the rules are **common sense**: we just need to behave sensibly. If something looks dangerous, **report it** to the person in charge (in the ICT room, that's your teacher).
Your data is your own, too. Be careful about where you share it and who you share your personal information with.
What is a hazard?

A **[[hazard]]** is a danger or risk: any source of potential **damage, harm or adverse (bad) health effects** on something or someone. Failing to stick to health and safety rules can result in injury.
Hazards in the ICT classroom

head: Hazard
What could happen
How to combat it
rows: Someone trips and falls, or pulls equipment off a desk
Tidy cables away under desks or in cable covers
Spills cause electric shocks or damage keyboards
No food or drink in the ICT room
Bags and coats on the floor
Put bags under desks, keep walkways clear
Don't plug too many devices into one socket; use proper extension leads
Don't touch it; report it to the teacher straight away
Room too hot, poor air flow
Open windows, use air conditioning or fans, keep vents clear
blocks.caption: Example hazards and solutions (the homework asks for five)

blocks.text: When you spot a hazard, think **Spot it, Stop it, Report it**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Keep three things safe: the equipment, our data and ourselves.
A hazard is any source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects.
Most safety rules are common sense.
If something looks dangerous, report it to the person in charge.

diagram.title: Spot it, Stop it, Report it
diagram.caption: What to do when you see a hazard.

items.label: Spot it
items.detail: Notice anything dangerous, like a loose cable or a spilled drink.

items.label: Stop it
items.detail: Stop using the equipment and warn people nearby. Don't try to fix electrics yourself.

items.label: Report it
items.detail: Tell the person in charge (your teacher) straight away.

items.label: Check it
items.detail: Once it's fixed, keep following the rules so it doesn't happen again.

check.why: Equipment, data and ourselves.

check.q: What is a hazard?
o: A source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects
check.why: That is the definition of a hazard.

practice.q: Identify **two** hazards in an ICT classroom and suggest a way to combat each one.
practice.a: e.g. trailing cables (1), tidy them away/use cable covers (1); drinks near computers (1), ban food and drink (1); bags on the floor (1), store under desks (1); overloaded sockets (1), use fewer plugs per socket (1).

pages.spec: Explain what causes backache when using computers and how to prevent it
pages.summary: Sitting in the same position for a long time, or on a chair at the wrong height, can cause backache and even damage the spine. Use an adjustable chair and a footrest, take regular breaks and don't slouch.

blocks.text: Back against the wall

**[[Backache]]** can be caused by sitting for long periods of time in the **same position**, or by having your **chair at the wrong height**. If this isn't dealt with, it could even cause **damage to the spine**.

Think about a long gaming session at home: hunched forward on the edge of the bed, staring at the TV for three hours. Your back is curved the whole time, and the next day it aches. The same thing can happen at a school or office desk.
How to combat backache

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: You can set the height and back support to fit your body.
Getting up and moving stops your muscles getting stiff.
If your feet don't reach the floor, a footrest supports your legs and back.
Good [[posture]] keeps your spine in its natural shape.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat backache

blocks.text: Good sitting posture

items: Sit back in the chair so your lower back is supported.
Keep your feet flat on the floor (or on a footrest).
Knees roughly level with your hips.
Shoulders relaxed, not hunched.
Screen at about eye level, straight in front of you.

blocks.text: Every 20–30 minutes, stand up, stretch and move about for a minute.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Backache is caused by sitting too long in one position or on a chair at the wrong height.
Left untreated, it can damage the spine.
Combat it with an adjustable chair, regular breaks, a footrest and good posture (no slouching).

check.q: What can cause backache when using a computer?
o: Sitting in the same position for a long time
check.why: Sitting too long in one position causes backache.

check.q: Which item helps a pupil whose feet don't reach the floor?
check.why: A footrest supports legs and back.

check.q: Which is good posture at a computer?
o: Back supported, feet flat, screen at eye level
Twisting to the side to see the screen
check.why: Supported back, flat feet and screen at eye level.

check.q: What serious problem could untreated backache lead to?
check.why: It can lead to damage to the spine.

practice.q: Describe **one** cause of backache when using a computer.
practice.a: Sitting in the same position for a long time / having a chair at the wrong height (1).
Use an adjustable chair (1); take regular breaks (1); use a footrest (1); change sitting position / don't slouch (1). Any three.

pages.spec: Explain what causes eye strain and how to prevent it
pages.summary: Eye strain is caused by looking at a screen for a long time, and glare from bright lights makes it worse. It can cause headaches, sore eyes and worse eyesight. Combat it with breaks, blinds, sensible screen positions and anti-glare screens.

blocks.text: A sight for sore eyes

**[[Eye strain]]** is caused by continuously looking at a screen for a long period of time. **Reflection** and **[[glare]]** from bright lights, such as sunlight shining on the screen, can make it worse.
Constantly straining your eyes can result in:

items: **Headaches**
**Sore eyes**
A **worsening of your eyesight**

blocks.text: How to combat eye strain

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: Text and images are big enough to read without squinting.
Gives your eyes a rest from focusing on the screen.
Stops bright sunlight causing glare on the screen.
Position your monitor away from direct sunlight
An [[anti-glare screen]] has a coating that cuts down reflections.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat eye strain

blocks.text: Try the **20-20-20 rule**: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Looking out the window towards the hills works well!
Phones count too. Scrolling for hours in bed in a dark room is a classic recipe for tired, sore eyes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Eye strain comes from looking at a screen for too long; glare and reflections make it worse.
It can cause headaches, sore eyes and worse eyesight.
Combat it with a suitable screen size, regular breaks, blinds, keeping the monitor out of direct sunlight and anti-glare screens.

check.q: What makes eye strain worse?
o: Reflection and glare from bright lights
check.why: Glare and reflections make eye strain worse.

check.q: Which is NOT a symptom of eye strain?
check.why: Numb thumbs are a sign of RSI.

check.q: Why should blinds be fitted to ICT room windows?
o: To stop sunlight causing glare on screens
To make the room darker for sleeping
check.why: Blinds reduce glare.

check.q: Where is the best place for a monitor?
check.why: Keep it out of direct sunlight.

practice.a: Looking continuously at a screen for a long period of time (made worse by glare/reflections) (1).

practice.q: Describe **three** ways to reduce eye strain.
practice.a: Any three: use a suitable screen size (1); take regular breaks (1); fit blinds to windows (1); position the monitor away from direct sunlight (1); use an anti-glare screen (1).

pages.spec: Explain what Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) is and how to prevent it
pages.summary: RSI happens when you make the same movement again and again, usually affecting the wrists and fingers. It can cause extreme pain and joint damage. Prevent it with an angled keyboard, a wrist rest, straight wrists and regular breaks.

blocks.text: Day after day after day
**[[Repetitive Strain Injury]]** (**RSI**) happens when you constantly make the **same movement** again and again. It usually affects the **joints in your wrists and fingers**.

Ever played a game for a long time and got sore or numb thumbs? This has been called **"Nintendo thumb"**. Typing, texting, clicking a mouse and pressing controller buttons are all repeated movements that can lead to RSI.
RSI can cause **extreme pain** and **damage to the joints**. In extreme cases it can lead to arthritis (painful, swollen joints).
How to combat RSI

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: Adjust your keyboard to a comfortable angle
Your hands and wrists aren't bent awkwardly.
A [[wrist rest]] supports your wrists so they stay straight.
Keep your wrists straight when typing
Bent wrists put extra strain on the joints.
Gives the muscles and joints a rest from repeating the same movement.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat RSI

blocks.title: Worked example: Conor's gaming marathon
blocks.context: Conor plays a football game on his console for four hours without stopping. His thumbs and wrists are sore and tingly the next day.
steps: The cause: repeating the same thumb movements for hours = a risk of RSI (Nintendo thumb).
Fix 1: take a break every 30–45 minutes and stretch his hands.
Fix 2: hold the controller in a relaxed way, keeping his wrists straight.
blocks.answer: Conor is showing early signs of RSI; regular breaks and good hand position will help.

blocks.title: Key points
items: RSI = Repetitive Strain Injury, caused by making the same movement again and again.
It usually affects joints in the wrists, fingers and thumbs ('Nintendo thumb').
It can cause extreme pain, joint damage and even arthritis.
Combat it with an angled keyboard, a wrist rest, straight wrists and regular breaks.

diagram.title: Match the health problem to the fix
diagram.caption: Click to match each problem with a way to combat it.
pairs: Use an adjustable chair and a footrest
Use an anti-glare screen and fit blinds
Use a wrist rest and keep wrists straight

check.q: What does RSI stand for?
check.why: RSI = Repetitive Strain Injury.

check.q: Which body parts does RSI usually affect?
check.why: RSI usually affects wrist and finger joints.

check.q: Which item helps prevent RSI?
check.why: A wrist rest keeps wrists supported and straight.

check.q: What is 'Nintendo thumb'?
o: Sore or numb thumbs from gaming for a long time
check.why: It is a form of RSI from gaming.

practice.a: Constantly making the same movement again and again (1), e.g. typing, clicking or pressing controller buttons, which strains the joints in the wrists/fingers (1).
Adjust keyboard to a comfortable angle (1); use a wrist rest (1); keep wrists straight when typing (1); take regular breaks (1). Any three.

pages.spec: Explain what ergonomics is and give examples of ergonomic design
pages.summary: Ergonomics is the science of designing safe, comfortable hardware and furniture for humans. Companies spend a lot on ergonomic controllers and chairs so people can use them longer, but you still need to look after your own health.

blocks.text: **[[Ergonomics]]** is the science concerned with designing **safe and comfortable hardware and office furniture for humans**. In other words, it is designing equipment that fits the human body.
Ergonomics in games consoles

items: PlayStation officially changed the design of its PS4 controller **three** times, and there are hundreds more controllers on the market.
Microsoft spent **"hundreds of millions"** designing its Xbox One controller.

blocks.text: Why spend so much? A comfortable controller means you can play for longer with less chance of getting sore or needing a break. That's good for the companies, because you keep using their products. **It's very important to remember to keep your own safety in mind** however comfortable the equipment feels.
Examples of ergonomic equipment

head: Equipment
Ergonomic feature
Problem it helps
rows: Height, back rest and arm rests can be changed
Supports feet that don't reach the floor
Screen angle and height can be adjusted
Eye strain, neck and back ache
Split or angled keys keep wrists straight
Soft support in front of keyboard or mouse
Fits the shape of the hand
blocks.caption: Ergonomic equipment

blocks.text: Even the shape of your phone, the angle of a laptop keyboard and the curve of a gaming chair are designed using ergonomics.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Ergonomics = designing safe and comfortable hardware and furniture for humans.
Sony redesigned the PS4 controller 3 times; Microsoft spent hundreds of millions on the Xbox One controller.
Ergonomic equipment includes adjustable chairs, footrests, tilting screens, wrist rests and shaped controllers.
Comfortable equipment helps, but you still need breaks and good habits.

diagram.title: An ergonomic workstation
diagram.caption: Click each part to see how it keeps you safe.

rows.label: Tilting screen at eye level
rows.detail: Can be angled away from glare; stops you bending your neck.

rows.label: Anti-glare filter
rows.detail: Reduces reflections that cause eye strain.

rows.label: Angled keyboard
rows.detail: Set at a comfortable angle so wrists stay straight.

rows.label: Wrist rest
rows.detail: Supports wrists to reduce the risk of RSI.

rows.label: Window blinds
rows.detail: Stop sunlight shining on the screen.

rows.label: Adjustable chair
rows.detail: Height and back support set to fit you, to prevent backache.

rows.label: Footrest
rows.detail: Supports your feet if they don't reach the floor.

check.q: What is ergonomics?
o: The science of designing safe, comfortable equipment for humans
A way to make computers faster
check.why: That is the definition of ergonomics.

check.q: How many times did PlayStation officially alter its PS4 controller?
check.why: It was altered three times.

check.q: Why do console companies spend so much on ergonomic controllers?
o: So you can play longer with less chance of getting sore
check.why: Comfortable products get used for longer.

check.q: Which is an example of ergonomic equipment?
check.why: An adjustable chair fits the user's body.

practice.a: The science concerned with designing safe and comfortable hardware and office furniture for humans (1).

practice.q: Give **two** examples of ergonomic equipment and explain how each one helps the user.
practice.a: e.g. adjustable chair (1), can be set to the right height to prevent backache (1); wrist rest (1), keeps wrists straight to prevent RSI (1); anti-glare screen (1), reduces reflections to prevent eye strain (1).

pages.spec: Describe threats to data and how to keep data safe
pages.summary: As well as protecting ourselves, we must protect our data. Threats include hackers, viruses, system crashes, accidental deletion and insider threats from employees. Backups, passwords, anti-virus software and good file management keep data safe.

blocks.text: As well as keeping ourselves protected when using ICT, we need to protect our **data** from being damaged. This is called **[[cyber security]]**. One big threat is the **[[hacker]]**: an unauthorised person who breaks into a system.
Threats to data

head: Threat
What happens
rows: Unauthorised users (hackers) gain access to data by illegal means.
Hackers often use viruses, which can attack and seriously damage files.
A crash affecting the hard drive may damage key sections of data.
Data can be lost accidentally or deleted by mistake.
Data can be sabotaged by former employees committing malicious (deliberately harmful) acts.
blocks.caption: Threats to our data

blocks.text: Insider threats

An **[[insider threat]]** comes from someone *inside* an organisation. It isn't always on purpose. Some employees cause damage by being **careless**, for example clicking a dodgy link or leaving a laptop on a bus. These careless insiders are sometimes called **pawns** or **goofs**, depending on the situation. You'll learn more about these at GCSE.
Keeping data safe: every problem has a solution

head: Problem
Solution
rows: Organise work in sensible folders with meaningful file names; use the computer's search tool to look for them.
Keep regular backups on another device or in the cloud (e.g. your school network area or Google Drive) so the work can be restored.
Use up-to-date anti-virus software to scan and remove it; restore a clean copy from a backup.
Search by date modified or by a word in the file; sort the folder by date; next time use meaningful names.
Password goes missing or is forgotten
Use the 'forgotten password' reset (or ask the network technician/teacher in school), then set a new strong password and never write it where others can see it.
blocks.caption: Keeping Data Safe: answers

blocks.text: The best protection against nearly every data problem is a **backup**: a second copy, kept somewhere else.

blocks.title: Key points
items: We must protect our data as well as ourselves.
Threats: hackers, viruses, system crashes, accidental loss and insider threats.
Insider threats can be deliberate or careless.
Backups, strong passwords, anti-virus software and organised folders keep data safe.

check.q: What is a hacker?
o: An unauthorised user who gains access to data illegally
check.why: Hackers gain unauthorised access.

check.q: An employee accidentally emails a customer list to the wrong person. What type of threat is this?
check.why: It is an insider threat, though not deliberate.

check.q: What is the best way to recover work after a computer is damaged?
check.why: Backups let you restore lost work.

check.q: Which of these is a threat to data?
check.why: Crashes can damage data on the hard drive.

practice.a: Any three: hackers gaining unauthorised access (1); viruses damaging files (1); system crashes damaging the hard drive (1); data lost or deleted by accident (1); sabotage by (former) employees / insider threats (1).

practice.q: Suggest a solution for each problem: (a) a file has a virus; (b) a computer is damaged.
practice.a: (a) Use up-to-date anti-virus software to scan/remove it (1); (b) restore the work from a backup (1).

pages.spec: Know the law on health and safety at work and eight things employers must do to keep ICT users safe
pages.summary: Employers have a duty of care to employees. The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and the Display Screen Equipment Regulations mean employers must provide things such as adjustable chairs, tiltable screens, anti-glare filters, breaks and eye tests.

blocks.text: Employers have a **[[duty of care]]** to their **[[employee|employees]]** when they use ICT. This means they are legally responsible for keeping them safe.
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

This is covered by the **[[Health and Safety at Work Act]]**, introduced in **1974**. It keeps employees, employers, data and equipment safe when people use ICT, or any computer-related equipment, as part of their job. It sets out the general duties that:

items: **employers** have towards employees and members of the public;
**employees** have to themselves and to each other;
certain **self-employed** people have towards themselves and others.

blocks.text: The Act provides the legal framework to promote, stimulate and encourage high standards of health and safety in workplaces. It protects employees and the public from work activities, including those that involve IT.

In Northern Ireland, the same duties come from the **Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978**, which matches the 1974 Act. The detailed rules for computer users are the **Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992**, which apply across the UK including NI.
Eight employer regulations for ICT users

head: Employers must…
This protects against…
rows: Eye strain, neck and back ache
Provide **foot supports** (footrests) for those who need them
Plan the work so employees get **regular breaks** or changes of activity
Pay for **eye tests** for regular screen users, and glasses if they are needed for screen work
Carry out **workstation assessments** and give **training** on safe use, with equipment such as wrist rests and suitable desks
RSI, backache and all other hazards
blocks.caption: Eight employer regulations

blocks.text: Notice that most regulations match the solutions you've already learned for backache, eye strain and RSI. Link each regulation to the health problem it prevents.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Employers have a duty of care to employees using ICT.
The Health and Safety at Work Act was introduced in 1974 (NI: the 1978 Order).
It sets duties for employers, employees and some self-employed people.
Employers must provide tiltable screens, anti-glare filters, adjustable chairs, footrests, breaks, eye tests, good lighting and training.

diagram.title: Which regulation prevents which problem?
diagram.caption: Click to reveal the answers.
head: Employer provides…
Helps prevent…
rows: Eye strain, neck and back ache

check.q: When was the Health and Safety at Work Act introduced?
check.why: It was introduced in 1974.

check.q: What does 'duty of care' mean for an employer?
o: They are legally responsible for keeping employees safe
They must give employees a car
check.why: A duty of care is a legal responsibility for safety.

check.q: Which employer regulation helps prevent eye strain?
check.why: Anti-glare filters reduce eye strain.

check.q: Who does the Act set duties for?
o: Employers, employees and some self-employed people
check.why: All three groups have duties.

practice.q: State **four** things an employer must provide to keep employees safe when using computers.
practice.a: Any four: tiltable screens (1); anti-glare filters (1); adjustable chairs (1); foot supports (1); regular breaks (1); eye tests (1); suitable lighting/blinds (1); training/workstation assessments (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an employer's **duty of care**.
practice.a: The employer has a legal responsibility (1) to look after the health and safety of their employees, e.g. when using ICT (1).

glossary.def: Rules and actions that protect people from injury or illness, at school or at work.
A danger or risk: any source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects on something or someone.
Pain in the back, which can be caused by sitting in the same position for a long time or on a chair at the wrong height.
The way you hold your body when sitting or standing.
Tired, sore eyes caused by looking at a screen for a long time, made worse by glare and reflections.
Bright light reflecting off a screen, making it hard to see and tiring your eyes.
A screen or filter with a special coating that reduces reflections and glare.
Pain and damage, usually in the wrists, fingers or thumbs, caused by making the same movement again and again.
A soft support placed in front of a keyboard or mouse to keep your wrists straight and supported.
The science of designing safe and comfortable hardware and office furniture for humans.
Protecting computers, networks and data from damage, theft or people who should not have access.
An unauthorised user who gains access to a computer system or data by illegal means.
A risk to data that comes from someone inside an organisation, such as a careless or angry employee.

glossary.term: Health and Safety at Work Act
glossary.def: The 1974 law that sets out the duties employers and employees have to keep people safe at work, including when using ICT.
A legal responsibility to look after the safety and wellbeing of others, such as an employer's duty to employees.
A person who works for an employer and is paid by them.
